sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 2:3-12 is the fullest picture of the end-time enemy in Paul. Before the day of the Lord come "the rebellion" and the revealing of "the man of lawlessness, the son of ruin" (the KJV's "man of sin", a later reading), who "lifts himself up over everything people call a god or worship" and sits "in the temple of God", claiming to be God (2:3-4). The language is Daniel's arrogant king (Daniel 11:36-37) and Ezekiel's ruler of Tyre (Ezekiel 28:2). He is held back for now, though "the mystery of lawlessness is at work already" (2:6-7); when revealed, he comes with Satan's power and false signs, and the Lord Jesus does away with him "by the breath of his mouth" and makes him powerless "by the appearing of his coming" (2:8; compare Isaiah 11:4). Paul does not use the word "antichrist".

The neuter "what is holding him back" (2:6) and the masculine "the one who is holding him back" (2:7) have been read as the Roman Empire and its emperor (Tertullian, Chrysostom), the Holy Spirit working through the church (dispensational teachers such as Thomas Ice), God or his plan, the preaching of the gospel, the archangel Michael (Daniel 12:1), or even a hostile power that "holds sway". Augustine, after listing the readings, wrote: "I frankly confess I do not know what he means" (City of God 20.19).

Irenaeus expected a single Antichrist in the Jerusalem Temple; Chrysostom saw Nero as his type. The Smalcald Articles (citing 2 Thessalonians 2:4), the Westminster Confession of 1646 (25.6) and the Second London Baptist Confession (26.4) identified the papacy as "that man of sin, and son of perdition"; later American Presbyterian revisions removed the line. The Catholic Catechism (675) speaks of the Antichrist's "pseudo-messianism", citing 2 Thessalonians 2:4-12, and names no one.

common: The man of lawlessness of 2 Thessalonians 2 is the same figure as the Antichrist of John's letters and the beast of Revelation 13.
uncommon: The restrainer of 2 Thessalonians 2:6-7 is the archangel Michael of Daniel 12:1.
"The rebellion" (apostasia) of 2 Thessalonians 2:3 means a physical departure, the rapture of the church.

sections.b: 2 Thessalonians uses three words for Christ's return: his "revealing" (apokalypsis) "from heaven with the angels of his power, in a flame of fire" (1:7-8), his "coming" (parousia, 2:1, 8), and "the appearing of his coming" (epiphaneia, 2:8). The return brings rest to the persecuted and judgment on their persecutors (1:6-10), and it ends the lawless one (2:8). The letter insists that it has not happened yet (2:2-3).

sections.h: 'The day of the Lord is already here'
sections.b: At Thessalonica someone claimed that "the day of the Lord is already here" (2 Thessalonians 2:2), with the perfect tense of a day that has arrived, not one that is near (the KJV's "at hand" misleads). The letter answers that the day cannot come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2:3). In chapter 1 the day is a day of glory for the saints and judgment for the persecutors, painted with Isaiah's day of the LORD (Isaiah 2:10, 19, 21; 66:15): "on that day" (1:10).

The letter speaks of "our gathering to him" (2:1) and says that the day of the Lord will not come until the rebellion and the man of lawlessness (2:3). Pre-tribulation teachers read the restrainer (2:6-7) as the Holy Spirit in the church, removed at the rapture before the lawless one appears; some, like Thomas Ice, read "the rebellion" (apostasia) as "the departure". Others answer that the gathering of 2:1 comes at the same coming that destroys the lawless one (2:8), after he is revealed, and that apostasia means revolt elsewhere (Acts 21:21; Joshua 22:22 in the Greek).

sections.h: The rebellion and the mystery of lawlessness
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians names a great "rebellion" (apostasia, 2:3) before the end, a revolt against God like those called by that word in the Greek of Joshua 22:22 and 1 Maccabees 2:15, and says that "the mystery of lawlessness is at work already" (2:7). The last days are already present in hidden form, but their climax is held back until God's time (2:6).

sections.h: Rest for the troubled, punishment for persecutors
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 1:5-10 describes God's "just judgment": those who trouble the church will receive trouble, and the troubled will be given rest, at the revealing of the Lord Jesus. The punishment falls on "people who do not know God" and "people who will not obey the good news" (1:8), perhaps the persecutors themselves, and is called "eternal ruin from the face of the Lord" (1:9), in the words of Isaiah 2:10. The Westminster Confession cites the passage in its chapter on the Last Judgment (33.2).

The phrase olethros aionios occurs only here (the Plain English Translation says "eternal ruin"). It is read as endless conscious punishment and separation from God (Catholic Catechism 1035; Westminster Confession 33.2, which quotes the verse), as final destruction in which the lost cease to exist (Seventh-day Adventist Fundamental Beliefs 27; Edward Fudge's conditional immortality), and by a few as a ruin from which God may still restore. The preposition "from the face of the Lord" can mean either separation from him or destruction coming from his presence.

sections.h: 'Sits in the temple of God' (2 Thessalonians 2:4)
sections.b: Paul's word is naos, the inner house of God. The man of lawlessness "sits down in the temple of God", claiming to be God. Readings: the Jerusalem Temple, still standing in the 50s (Irenaeus; and the memory of Caligula's order of AD 40 to put his statue there); a temple rebuilt in the future (dispensational teachers); the church, God's temple in Paul's other letters (1 Corinthians 3:16; the Reformers applied this to the papacy); or a picture of claiming God's throne (Ezekiel 28:2). Augustine said it was "uncertain in what temple he shall sit".

2 Thessalonians 2:13 uses a rare verb for God's choice, heilato, the form found in the Greek of Deuteronomy 26:18 for the LORD choosing Israel as his own people. God chose the readers "for salvation, by the Spirit who makes you holy and by faith in the truth", in contrast with those who refused the love of the truth (2:10-12). The manuscripts divide between "as firstfruits" and "from the beginning" (see the variant).

If the reading "as firstfruits" is right at 2 Thessalonians 2:13 (the SBL and NA28 editions print it; THGNT and the Byzantine text read "from the beginning"), the Thessalonians are the first sheaf of a harvest in Macedonia, as Epaenetus was "the firstfruits of Asia" (Romans 16:5).

"Keep a firm grip on the traditions you were taught, whether we taught them by speaking or in our letter" (2:15). The Second Vatican Council quotes the verse for apostolic Tradition alongside Scripture (Dei Verbum 8); Protestant confessions answer that Scripture alone is now the rule (Formula of Concord; Westminster Confession 1.6, which cites 2 Thessalonians 2:2 among its proofs; Second London Baptist Confession 1.1, 1.6). In 3:6 the same word means Paul's teaching about work.

sections.h: 'Whoever does not want to work should not eat either'
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 3:6-12 commands members who live "out of line" and refuse to work to "work quietly and eat bread that is their own", pointing to Paul's own example of working night and day (3:8). The rule concerns those who will not work, not those who cannot. Explanations of the idleness: end-time excitement (2:2), or a social problem of poor members living on richer ones (R. Russell). The saying was later quoted by Lenin (The State and Revolution, 1917) and in article 12 of the 1936 Soviet constitution.

sections.h: 'Do not treat him like an enemy'
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 3:6 and 3:14-15 tell the church to keep apart from a member who refuses to obey the letter, to "mark that person out" and not "mix with him" (the verb of 1 Corinthians 5:9, 11), so that he will feel shame, but not to treat him as an enemy: "Correct him as a brother." The Westminster Confession (30.4) and the Dordrecht Confession (1632, article 17) both cite these verses, the first for censures by the elders, the second for shunning that admonishes the shunned "as brethren".

The lawless one's coming is "driven by Satan's working, with every kind of power, and with signs and wonders that are a lie" (2:9). The same word, energeia, describes the "working that leads them astray" that God sends on those who refused the truth (2:11). The letter also prays that the Lord will keep the readers "safe from the evil one" (3:3).

2 Thessalonians shows the church still under persecution (1:4), unsettled by a claim that the day of the Lord had come (2:2), and troubled by members who had stopped working (3:6-12). It was probably written from Corinth soon after 1 Thessalonians, if Paul wrote it.

2 Thessalonians ends: "The greeting is in my own hand, Paul's. That is the sign in every letter: I write like this" (3:17), the same first sentence as 1 Corinthians 16:21. Paul dictated his letters and signed them; here the signature answers a letter "that seems to be from us" (2:2). Whether Paul himself wrote this letter is disputed: see the 2-thessalonians topic.
Silvanus is named with Paul and Timothy at the head of 2 Thessalonians (1:1), as in 1 Thessalonians 1:1, because he helped found the church (Acts 17:4).

Timothy is named with Paul and Silvanus at the head of 2 Thessalonians (1:1). He had been sent back to Thessalonica to strengthen the church (1 Thessalonians 3:2), and on one view (Wanamaker) carried this letter to them.

The man of lawlessness who "lifts himself up over everything people call a god or worship" (2 Thessalonians 2:4) is drawn from Daniel's king who "will lift himself above everything" (Daniel 11:37; compare Daniel 11:36 and Daniel 7:25). The Greek of Theodotion's Daniel 11:36 has the same phrase as Paul, "over every god".

sections.h: A man in the temple of God
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 2:4 does not use the phrase, but its picture of a figure who takes his seat "in the temple of God" claiming to be God continues the line from Daniel's abomination that desolates (Daniel 9:27; 11:31; 12:11), set up by Antiochus IV, through Jesus' warning (Matthew 24:15; Mark 13:14), with Caligula's attempt of AD 40 as a recent memory.

sections.h: A short apocalypse in a letter
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 2:1-12 has the marks of Jewish apocalyptic writing: a fixed order of events before the end, a hidden evil already at work, a restraining power, a revealing, a final enemy who claims divine honor, and his sudden defeat by God's agent. 1:7-10 adds a judgment scene built from Isaiah. The passage assumes fuller oral teaching (2:5) that later readers do not have.

sections.h: 'God sends them a working that leads them astray'
sections.b: Those who "did not accept the love of the truth" are given over to it: "God sends them a working that leads them astray, and so they come to believe the lie" (2 Thessalonians 2:10-11). As with Pharaoh, and with the lying spirit sent to Ahab's prophets (1 Kings 22:22), God's act follows and confirms the people's own refusal.

sections.h: Suffering as a sign of God's justice
sections.b: 2 Thessalonians 1:4-7 calls the believers' endurance under persecution "a plain sign of God's just judgment": they suffer for God's kingdom, and God will give them rest and repay those who trouble them when the Lord Jesus is revealed.

Three chapters, three answers: God's justice for the persecuted (chapter 1), "not yet" for those told the day had come (chapter 2), and "work quietly" for those who had stopped working (chapter 3), closed with Paul's own signature (3:17).
